title: Daily reading
tomorrow: Dad says sadaqah has to be money. what if you're broke till payday?

segments.voice: The evening adhkar: the morning's words turned toward the dark, and a scorpion story on Dadi's porch. Evening, remembered. Now, the reading that fits between the posts.

New-year plans have a way of dying in the first week: the gym, the journal, the whole Qur'an over winter break. It's day four, and the plan is three days behind. Quit, or cram? Here's something odd in the Qur'an itself. Surah al-Muzzammil opens by asking the Prophet ﷺ to stand much of the night in prayer and recitation. Then its last verse, one long verse, says the same short thing twice: recite of the Qur'an what is easy for you. Why say it twice?
screen: `DAY FOUR, THREE DAYS BEHIND.` → `QUIT, OR CRAM?` → `ONE VERSE SAYS IT TWICE.`

segments.voice: Read what sits between the two. In the middle of that verse, the Qur'an names the reasons a long night of reading won't always fit: some of you are sick, some travel the land looking for a living, some are fighting in God's cause. Real lives, named one by one. Then, again: so recite of it what is easy. The repeat isn't a typo. It's the ease arriving after the reasons, so nobody misses it. That's the root of a wird: a daily portion, a set amount of Qur'an someone returns to every day. A page, a few verses, a section. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says the deeds most loved by God are the ones done most constantly, even if they're small. And there's a story about pushing too hard. A young companion, Abdullah ibn Amr, was reading the whole Qur'an every night. The Prophet told him once a month. Abdullah bargained for more, and more, until the Prophet said: then in seven, and no faster. Years later, an old man, Abdullah said he wished he'd accepted the easier one. So the puzzle has an answer for day four. Not quit, not cram. Make the portion smaller, and make it daily.
screen: `THE REASONS, NAMED.` · `WHAT IS EASY, SAID TWICE.` · `SMALL, AND CONSTANT.` · `ABDULLAH WISHED HE'D TAKEN IT EASY.` · then, large: `MY PORTION.`

segments.voice: Open whatever you read from, a Qur'an, a translation, any book you keep coming back to, and choose one short line. Read it out loud, slowly, then once more even slower. Then sit with the second reading still in your ears.
screen: `ONE SHORT LINE.` · `OUT LOUD, SLOWLY.` · `ONCE MORE, SLOWER.`

howItsDone: Muslims who keep a wird, a fixed daily portion of the Qur'an, often read a page or a section after Fajr or before sleep; printed copies are divided into parts that make a steady pace easy to track.

fork.setup: your dad works twelve-hour days at his shop and wants to start reading Qur'an daily. he asks you what a realistic wird is.
options: a big section a day, so he finishes fast and feels it.
nothing until the shop slows down and he has real time.
a page or a few verses he can keep every single day.
fork.reveal: the verse names real lives, work included, and says recite what is easy. small and constant is what the hadith says God loves.

original.note: Arabic: a regular portion, a set amount of Qur'an or dhikr kept daily.

trapdoor: what you thought: reading the whole Qur'an as fast as you can.
what it means: a small daily portion, kept every day, shaped to a real life.
what a scholar hears: 73:20's double fa-qra'u ma tayassara, Bukhari 6464 on constant deeds, and Abdullah ibn Amr's regret in Bukhari 5052.

chat.says: planned the whole quran over break. day 4, already 3 days behind. should i just quit?
options: Shrink it to a portion that's easy, and keep it every day.
Double up tonight and catch up; finishing is the whole point.
Stop for now and start fresh in Ramadan, when it's easier.
chat.meaning: The Qur'an says recite what is easy, twice, and the hadith says small and constant is most loved. Smaller, and daily.

wird.meaning: a daily portion of Qur'an or remembrance, kept regularly

al-Muzzammil.meaning: 'the enwrapped one': the name of surah 73

Abdullah ibn Amr.meaning: a young companion of the Prophet who loved long worship

Sahih al-Bukhari.meaning: a major collection of the Prophet's sayings

sources.ref: Qur'an 73:1–4, 73:20 (stand much of the night; recite of the Qur'an what is easy, said twice in 73:20)

Sahih al-Bukhari 5052, 5054 (Abdullah ibn Amr: finish in a month, bargained to seven; his regret in old age)

Abdullah ibn Amr's story: Bukhari 5052 (with his regret in old age) and 5054 (the bargaining to seven); confirm numbers and that 'reading the whole Qur'an every night' matches the report.
